title: The Easter homily
hookLine: his short Easter sermon, still read at Orthodox Easter: come, the first and the last

cards: Past midnight, deep into the Easter night service. Candles everywhere, people shoulder to shoulder, some worn out from the long fast, some who didn't fast at all and just walked in off the street.
Then the priest reads a short sermon. Orthodox churches, and Eastern Catholic churches of the same Byzantine tradition, read it on Easter night, and tradition gives it to John Chrysostom.
It speaks straight to the person at the back who feels they don't belong here tonight.

teach.b: First, the welcome. The sermon calls in everyone who loves God to enjoy this bright feast. Then it starts counting the hours, and you realize where you are: the parable of the workers in the vineyard, from Matthew.
Some started at dawn. Some at the third hour, the sixth, the ninth. Some came at the eleventh hour, with barely any day left.
Second, the surprise. In Jesus's parable, the landowner pays everyone the same, and the early workers grumble. The homily turns that story into an invitation.
If you came at the eleventh hour, it says, don't be afraid because you're late. The Master is generous.

teach.h: THE LAST, JUST AS THE FIRST.
teach.b: He receives the last just as the first. He welcomes the deed, and honors even the intention. Third, the table.
You who fasted and you who did not, the homily says, rejoice today.
The table is full. Let no one go away hungry. Nobody is checking who earned a seat.
Fourth, why. Because of what Easter is. The homily ends by turning to death itself, in Paul's words.
In the Douay-Rheims: "O death, where is thy victory? O death, where is thy sting?" Christ is risen, it says, and life reigns. So in the homily the generosity isn't a mood.
It comes from the empty tomb: if death has lost, there's no reason to turn latecomers away.
The eleventh hour, too, gets the full wage.

how: In Orthodox and Byzantine Catholic churches the Paschal homily attributed to John Chrysostom is read aloud at the Easter night service, and some Latin-rite Catholics read it during the Easter season.

games.why: don't be afraid because you're late, it says. the table is full; let no one go away hungry.

practice: Think of someone who arrived late to something you're part of: the new person on the team, a cousin who missed years of family dinners, a neighbor who just moved in, someone back at church after a long time away.
Hold their face a moment and think of one small way to say, the table is full, there's room for you. If you pray, thank God for the ones who welcomed you when you were late.

wordCard.voice: Pascha. The Church's Greek name for Easter, and the night the homily tradition gives to Chrysostom welcomes even the eleventh hour's workers. Today's word.
